title: Variables & Scope
tagline: Storing values and knowing where they live

items.title: let
items.explain: Declares a variable that can be reassigned later.

items.title: const
items.explain: Declares a variable that cannot be reassigned (objects/arrays inside it can still be mutated).

items.title: Global Scope
items.explain: A variable declared outside any function is reachable from anywhere in the file.

items.title: Block Scope
items.explain: let and const only exist inside the { } block they were declared in.

items.title: Hoisting
items.explain: JavaScript moves declarations to the top of their scope, but let/const stay uninitialized until their line runs.

title: Data Types
tagline: Every value in JS is either primitive or a reference

items.title: Number
items.explain: Represents both integers and decimals as a single numeric type.

items.title: String
items.explain: Text data, wrapped in quotes, with built-in methods for reading and transforming it.

items.title: Boolean
items.explain: Only two possible values: true or false.

items.title: Undefined
items.explain: The default value of a variable that has been declared but not assigned.

items.title: Null
items.explain: Represents an intentional empty value, set explicitly by the developer.

items.title: BigInt
items.explain: Stores integers larger than Number can safely represent.

items.title: Symbol
items.explain: Creates a guaranteed unique identifier, often used as a hidden object key.

items.title: Object / Array / Function
items.explain: The three reference types: objects group data, arrays order it, functions act on it.

items.title: typeof
items.explain: Returns a string naming the type of a value; famously reports "object" for null.

title: Operators
tagline: The symbols that combine, compare, and transform values

items.title: Arithmetic
items.explain: Perform math: add, subtract, multiply, divide, remainder, and exponent.

items.title: Assignment
items.explain: Assign a value, optionally combined with an operation (+=, -=, etc).
items.code:
let x = 10;
x += 5; // same as x = x + 5

items.title: Comparison (== vs ===)
items.explain: == converts types before comparing; === checks value and type together. Prefer ===.

items.title: Logical (&&, ||, !, ??)
items.explain: Combine boolean expressions; ?? returns the right side only when the left is null/undefined.

items.title: Increment / Decrement
items.explain: x++ returns the value then increases it; ++x increases it then returns the value.

items.title: Ternary
items.explain: A compact one-line if/else that evaluates to a value.

items.title: Bitwise
items.explain: Operate on the individual bits of a number: AND, OR, XOR, NOT, shifts.

items.title: Spread / Rest (...)
items.explain: Spread expands an iterable into elements; rest collects extra arguments into an array.

items.title: Optional Chaining (?.)
items.explain: Safely reads a nested property, returning undefined instead of throwing if a link is missing.

items.title: Nullish Coalescing Assignment (??=)
items.explain: Assigns a value only if the variable is currently null or undefined.

items.title: typeof / instanceof
items.explain: Check a value's primitive type, or whether it was built from a specific constructor.

items.title: delete / in / new
items.explain: delete removes a property, in checks for its existence, new constructs an instance.

items.title: Comma & Grouping
items.explain: The comma operator evaluates multiple expressions; parentheses group and control precedence.

title: Type Conversion
tagline: Changing a value from one type into another

items.title: String Conversion
items.explain: Explicitly turns any value into its string representation.

items.title: Number Conversion
items.explain: Turns a value into a number, or NaN if it can't be parsed.

items.title: Boolean Conversion & Truthy/Falsy
items.explain: false, 0, "", null, undefined, and NaN convert to false; everything else converts to true.

items.title: Implicit Conversion
items.explain: JavaScript automatically converts types in mixed operations, which can surprise you.

items.title: Interpolation
items.explain: Backtick strings can embed variables and expressions directly with ${ }.

items.title: Multi-line Strings
items.explain: Backtick strings preserve line breaks without needing \n.

items.title: Expressions Inside
items.explain: Any valid JS expression can go inside ${ }, including math.

title: Comments
tagline: Notes in code that JavaScript ignores

items.title: Single Line
items.explain: Everything after // on a line is ignored.

items.title: Multi Line
items.explain: Everything between /* and */ is ignored, even across lines.

items.title: Documentation Style
items.explain: A /** */ block just above a function, commonly used to describe what it does.

title: Conditionals
tagline: Branching code based on a condition

items.title: if
items.explain: Runs a block of code only when its condition is truthy.

items.title: else
items.explain: Runs its block when the if condition was false.

items.title: else if
items.explain: Checks additional conditions in order until one is true.

items.title: Nested if
items.explain: An if statement placed inside another if's block for combined conditions.

items.title: switch
items.explain: Compares one value against many possible cases, an alternative to long else-if chains.

items.title: switch Fall-through
items.explain: Without break, execution continues into the next case instead of stopping.

items.title: Grouping switch Cases
items.explain: Stacking case labels without a break between them lets them share one block.

items.title: Ternary as if/else
items.explain: A single-line stand-in for a simple if/else that returns a value.

items.title: Nested Ternary
items.explain: Chaining ternaries to check multiple conditions — readable in small doses only.

title: Loops
tagline: Repeating code until a condition ends

items.title: for
items.explain: Repeats a fixed number of times using an initializer, condition, and update step.

items.title: Nested for
items.explain: A loop inside another loop, useful for grids and combinations.

items.title: while
items.explain: Repeats as long as its condition stays true, checked before each run.

items.title: do...while
items.explain: Runs the block once first, then repeats while the condition holds.

items.title: for...of
items.explain: Loops over the values of an iterable: arrays, strings, Maps, Sets.

items.title: for...in
items.explain: Loops over the enumerable keys of an object.

items.title: break
items.explain: Immediately exits the loop entirely.

items.title: continue
items.explain: Skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one.

items.title: Labels
items.explain: Names a loop so break/continue can target an outer loop from within a nested one. Rarely used.

items.title: Function Declaration
items.explain: Defines a named, reusable block of code with the function keyword.

items.title: Function Declarations Are Hoisted
items.explain: A function declaration can be called before it appears in the file.

items.title: Parameters vs Arguments
items.explain: Parameters are the named placeholders in the definition; arguments are the actual values passed in.

items.title: Default Parameters
items.explain: Gives a parameter a fallback value used when no argument is passed.

items.title: Rest Parameters
items.explain: Collects any number of extra arguments into a single array.

items.title: return
items.explain: Sends a value back to the caller and immediately stops the function.

items.title: Function Expression
items.explain: Stores a function inside a variable; unlike declarations, it is not hoisted.

items.title: Arrow Functions
items.explain: A shorter function syntax, commonly used throughout React for callbacks and handlers.
items.code:
const add = (a, b) => a + b;
const square = x => x * x;

items.title: Arrow Returning an Object
items.explain: Wrap an object literal in parentheses so it isn't mistaken for a function body.

items.title: Arrow Functions Have No Own this
items.explain: Arrow functions inherit this from their surrounding scope instead of the object that calls them.

items.title: IIFE
items.explain: A function that runs immediately after being defined, often used to create an isolated scope.

items.title: call / apply / bind
items.explain: Control what this refers to inside a function when invoking or pre-configuring it.

items.title: Recursion
items.explain: A function that calls itself until it reaches a base case that stops it.

title: Scope & Closures
tagline: How JavaScript remembers variables across function calls

items.title: Lexical Scope
items.explain: An inner function can access variables from the outer function that contains it.

items.title: Scope Chain
items.explain: When a variable isn't found locally, JS searches outward: local → parent → global.

items.title: Closures
items.explain: A function keeps access to its outer variables even after the outer function has finished running.

items.title: Private Variables via Closure
items.explain: A closure can hide a variable so it's only reachable through returned methods, not directly.

items.title: Closures in Loops: var vs let
items.explain: var shares one variable across all iterations; let creates a fresh binding each time, which is usually what you want.

title: Higher-Order Functions & Callbacks
tagline: Functions that take or return other functions

items.title: Callback Function
items.explain: A function passed as an argument to another function, to be run later, often after some work finishes.

items.title: HOF Taking a Function
items.explain: A higher-order function accepts another function as one of its arguments.

items.title: HOF Returning a Function
items.explain: A higher-order function can also build and return a new, customized function.

items.title: setTimeout
items.explain: Schedules a callback to run once after a delay, without blocking the rest of the code.

title: Arrays
tagline: Ordered lists of values, indexed from 0

items.title: Creating Arrays
items.explain: The array literal [ ] is the standard, most common way to create an array.

items.title: Access & Modify
items.explain: Elements are read and written using their zero-based index.

items.title: push() / pop()
items.explain: push adds to the end of the array; pop removes the last element.

items.title: unshift() / shift()
items.explain: unshift adds to the beginning; shift removes the first element.
items.code:
arr.unshift(0); // add to start
arr.shift();    // remove from start

items.title: forEach()
items.explain: Runs a function once for every element; cannot break or return a new array.

items.title: map()
items.explain: Transforms every element and returns a brand-new array, leaving the original untouched. Used constantly in React to render lists.

items.title: filter()
items.explain: Returns a new array containing only the elements that pass a test.

items.title: reduce()
items.explain: Collapses an array down to a single value by running an accumulator function over each element.

items.title: find() / findIndex()
items.explain: find returns the first matching element (or undefined); findIndex returns its position instead.

items.title: some() / every()
items.explain: some checks if at least one element passes a test; every checks if all of them do.

items.title: sort()
items.explain: Sorts an array in place; without a compare function it sorts as strings, so numbers need one.

items.title: slice()
items.explain: Extracts a section of an array into a new array, without changing the original.

items.title: splice()
items.explain: Adds, removes, or replaces elements directly inside the original array.
items.code:
arr.splice(1, 2);      // remove 2 items starting at index 1
arr.splice(1, 0, 99);  // insert 99 at index 1
arr.splice(1, 1, 99);  // replace item at index 1

items.title: concat() / includes() / indexOf()
items.explain: concat merges arrays; includes checks for a value; indexOf finds a value's position.

items.title: reverse() / join()
items.explain: reverse flips the array order in place; join turns an array into a string with a chosen separator.

items.title: flat()
items.explain: Flattens nested arrays into a single level, up to the depth you specify.

items.title: Array Destructuring
items.explain: Unpacks array values into individual variables in one line.

items.title: Spread Operator
items.explain: Expands an array's elements, useful for copying or merging arrays.

items.title: Array.from() / Array.isArray()
items.explain: Array.from converts an iterable into a real array; Array.isArray checks if a value is one.

items.title: Nested Arrays
items.explain: Arrays can contain other arrays, accessed by chaining index brackets.

title: Objects
tagline: Key-value collections for grouping related data

items.title: Creating Objects
items.explain: The object literal { } is the standard way to group related key-value pairs.
items.code:
let user = { name: "Sajin", age: 19 };
let empty = {};

items.title: Dot vs Bracket Notation
items.explain: Dot notation is used for known property names; brackets are required for dynamic or variable keys.
items.code:
person.name;      // dot
person["name"];   // bracket
let key = "age";
person[key];       // dynamic key needs brackets

items.title: Modify / Add / Delete
items.explain: Properties can be changed, added, or removed at any time after creation.

items.title: Nested Objects
items.explain: Objects can contain other objects or arrays, accessed by chaining.
items.code:
let user = { name: "Sajin", address: { city: "Pammal" } };
user.address.city;

items.title: Optional Chaining
items.explain: Safely reads a deeply nested property without throwing if a link along the way is missing.

items.title: Methods & this
items.explain: A function stored as an object property; this inside it refers to the object that called it.

items.title: Object.keys() / values() / entries()
items.explain: Return an object's keys, its values, or [key, value] pairs as arrays for looping.
items.code:
let user = { name: "A", age: 20 };
Object.keys(user);    // ["name", "age"]
Object.values(user);  // ["A", 20]
Object.entries(user); // [["name","A"],["age",20]]

items.title: Object Destructuring
items.explain: Extracts properties into standalone variables, with optional renaming and default values.

items.title: Spread & Rest
items.explain: Spread copies or merges an object's properties; rest gathers the remaining ones into a new object.

items.title: Objects Are References
items.explain: Assigning an object to a new variable copies the reference, not the data — both point to the same object.

items.title: Object.freeze() / seal()
items.explain: freeze blocks all changes; seal blocks adding or removing properties but still allows editing existing ones.

items.title: structuredClone()
items.explain: Creates a true, independent deep copy of an object, including nested structures.

items.title: Object ↔ JSON
items.explain: Convert an object to a JSON string and back using the built-in JSON methods.

items.title: Object.hasOwn() / Object.assign()
items.explain: hasOwn checks if a property truly belongs to the object; assign merges multiple objects into one.

items.title: Shorthand & Computed Properties
items.explain: Shorthand skips repeating a key and variable of the same name; computed properties use a variable as the key.

title: DOM Manipulation
tagline: Reading and changing HTML from JavaScript

items.title: getElementById()
items.explain: Selects a single element by its id attribute.

items.title: querySelector()
items.explain: Selects the first element matching any CSS selector — the most flexible and commonly used selector.

items.title: querySelectorAll()
items.explain: Selects every matching element and returns a NodeList you can loop over with forEach.

items.title: getElementsByClassName() / TagName()
items.explain: Older selection methods that return a live HTMLCollection instead of a static NodeList.

items.title: textContent
items.explain: Reads or sets an element's text, treating anything you assign as plain text (safe from HTML injection).
items.code:
p.textContent = "

Hi

"; // inserted literally as text, not rendered as HTML

items.title: innerHTML
items.explain: Reads or sets an element's content and parses it as HTML — powerful but risky with untrusted input.
items.code: p.innerHTML = "Welcome"; // renders as bold text // Avoid: element.innerHTML = userInput; (XSS risk)

items.title: innerText
items.explain: Reads only the text that is actually visible on the page, ignoring hidden elements.

items.title: setAttribute / getAttribute / removeAttribute
items.explain: The generic way to read, write, or remove any HTML attribute.

items.title: element.style
items.explain: Sets CSS properties directly on an element, inline — quick, but gets messy at scale.

items.title: classList (add / remove / toggle / contains)
items.explain: The recommended way to manage styles: toggle predefined CSS classes instead of individual style properties.

items.title: createElement() + append()
items.explain: Builds a new element in memory, then inserts it into the page.

items.title: append / prepend / before / after
items.explain: Insert content at the end, the start, or immediately beside a reference element.
items.code:
parent.append(child);   // end
parent.prepend(child);  // start
el.before(newEl);       // just before
el.after(newEl);        // just after

items.title: insertAdjacentHTML()
items.explain: Inserts raw HTML at a precise position relative to an element without replacing existing content.
items.code:
element.insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend", "

Hi

"); // positions: beforebegin, afterbegin, beforeend, afterend

items.title: cloneNode()
items.explain: Creates a copy of an element; pass true to also copy its children.

items.title: remove() / removeChild() / replaceWith()
items.explain: Three ways to take an element out of the page, or swap it for another.

items.title: DOM Traversal
items.explain: Move between related elements: parent, children, and siblings.

items.title: addEventListener()
items.explain: Attaches a function that runs whenever a specific event happens on an element. The foundation of interactivity — and of how React thinks about events.

items.title: The Event Object
items.explain: Automatically passed into every handler, carrying details about what happened.

items.title: event.preventDefault()
items.explain: Stops the browser's default behavior for an event, like a form submitting and reloading the page.

items.title: Event Bubbling
items.explain: A triggered event travels upward from the target element through each of its ancestors.

items.title: Event Delegation
items.explain: One listener on a parent handles events for all its (even future) children, by checking event.target.

items.title: Forms & input.value
items.explain: Read what a user typed via .value, and prevent the page from reloading on submit.

items.title: DOMContentLoaded
items.explain: Waits until the HTML is fully parsed before running code, so elements are guaranteed to exist.

items.title: focus() / blur() / scrollIntoView() / contains()
items.explain: Common utility methods: move focus, remove focus, scroll an element into view, or check ancestry.

title: Error Handling
tagline: Catching problems before they crash your program

items.title: Types of Errors
items.explain: Syntax errors break parsing, runtime errors happen while executing, logical errors run fine but give wrong results.

items.title: try...catch
items.explain: Runs risky code in try; if it throws, execution jumps to catch instead of crashing the program.

items.title: The Error Object
items.explain: catch receives an error object with name, message, and stack properties describing what went wrong.

items.title: throw
items.explain: Manually raises an error, either as a value or (better) as an Error instance.

items.title: Built-in Error Types
items.explain: Specific error subclasses: TypeError, ReferenceError, SyntaxError, RangeError, URIError.
items.code:
new TypeError();      // wrong type used
new ReferenceError(); // variable doesn't exist
new RangeError();     // value out of range

items.title: finally
items.explain: Runs after try/catch regardless of whether an error occurred — ideal for cleanup.

items.title: Custom Error Classes
items.explain: Extend the built-in Error class to create your own named, reusable error types.

items.title: Async Error Handling
items.explain: Catch errors from Promises with .catch(), or with try/catch around an await.

items.title: Error Propagation
items.explain: An uncaught error keeps moving up the call stack until a try/catch handles it.

title: Promises
tagline: Representing a value that will be available later

items.title: new Promise()
items.explain: Wraps async work in an object that will eventually resolve (succeed) or reject (fail).

items.title: reject() & .catch()
items.explain: Signals failure with reject, and handles it downstream with .catch().

items.title: A Promise Object Itself
items.explain: Calling a function that returns a Promise doesn't give you the value directly — it gives a pending Promise you must resolve.

items.title: fs.promises (Node.js)
items.explain: Node's promise-based file system API lets you read files with .then() instead of error-first callbacks.

items.title: async/await with fs
items.explain: The cleanest way to read files: await pauses until the Promise resolves.

items.title: Promise.all()
items.explain: Runs multiple Promises in parallel and waits for all of them to finish, which is faster than awaiting one at a time.

title: Fetch, HTTP & APIs
tagline: Talking to servers from the browser

items.title: What is an API?
items.explain: An interface that lets your app request or send data to a server, which usually talks to a database.
items.code:
// Browser → API → Server → Database
// Examples: weather apps, social feeds, maps

items.title: REST API Basics
items.explain: REST APIs organize data behind predictable URLs called endpoints, manipulated with HTTP methods.

items.title: GET — Read Data
items.explain: Requests existing data from the server without modifying anything.

items.title: POST — Create Data
items.explain: Sends a new piece of data to the server to be created, typically with a JSON body.

items.title: PUT vs PATCH
items.explain: PUT replaces an entire resource; PATCH updates only the fields you send.
items.code:
fetch(url, { method: "PUT", body: JSON.stringify(fullData) });
fetch(url, { method: "PATCH", body: JSON.stringify({ name: "New" }) });

items.title: DELETE — Remove Data
items.explain: Requests that a resource be removed from the server.

items.title: fetch()
items.explain: The built-in function for making HTTP requests; it always returns a Promise.

items.title: async/await with fetch
items.explain: A cleaner alternative to chaining .then(), pausing execution until each step completes.

items.title: Headers
items.explain: Metadata sent with a request, such as the format of the data you're sending.

items.title: The Response Object
items.explain: What fetch resolves to; check res.ok or res.status before reading the body.

items.title: Status Codes
items.explain: Numeric codes describing the outcome of a request: 200s succeed, 400s are client errors, 500s are server errors.
items.code:
200 OK          201 Created
400 Bad Request 401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden   404 Not Found
500 Server Error

items.title: Query Parameters
items.explain: Extra key-value data appended to a URL after a ?, used to filter or specify a request.

items.title: Handling fetch Errors
items.explain: fetch only rejects on network failure — check res.ok yourself to catch HTTP error responses like 404.

items.title: localStorage + JSON
items.explain: Browser storage only holds strings, so objects must be stringified before saving and parsed after reading.

title: JSON
tagline: The universal text format for exchanging data

items.title: What is JSON?
items.explain: A lightweight, text-based data format that looks like a JavaScript object but follows stricter rules.

items.title: JSON Rules
items.explain: Keys and strings must use double quotes; functions and comments are not allowed.

items.title: JS Object vs JSON
items.explain: A JS object is a live in-memory structure; JSON is its text-based, portable equivalent.
items.code:
let user = { name: "Sajin" }; // object, usable in JS
'{"name":"Sajin"}';           // JSON, a text string

items.title: JSON.stringify()
items.explain: Converts a JavaScript object into a JSON-formatted string, ready to send or store.

items.title: JSON.parse()
items.explain: Converts a JSON string back into a usable JavaScript object.

items.title: Pretty Printing
items.explain: Pass an indent value as the third argument to stringify to format JSON for human reading.

title: Modules
tagline: Splitting code across files and reusing it

items.title: What is a Module?
items.explain: A JavaScript file with its own private scope, whose values can be shared using export/import.

items.title: export / import
items.explain: export makes a value available outside its file; import brings it into another file.

items.title: Named Exports
items.explain: Export multiple values by name from one file; import them using matching names in curly braces.

items.title: Renaming Exports
items.explain: Use the as keyword to give an export or import a different local name.

items.title: Default Exports
items.explain: Each module can have exactly one default export, imported without curly braces and any name you choose.

items.title: Named + Default Together
items.explain: A single file can mix one default export with several named exports.

items.title: Import Everything (* as)
items.explain: Imports every export from a module bundled together as one object.

items.title: Dynamic import()
items.explain: Loads a module on demand at runtime, returning a Promise — useful for code-splitting.

items.title: Browser Modules
items.explain: The type="module" attribute enables import/export syntax directly in browser scripts.

items.title: Node.js Modules: ESM vs CommonJS
items.explain: Node supports modern import/export (ESM) alongside the older require() syntax (CommonJS).
